newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Foreign banks face uphill struggle in Slovenia.
newsitem.headline: Foreign banks face uphill struggle in Slovenia.

text.p: Slovenia boasts sound economic growth, a stable currency and excellent international credit ratings while its two million inhabitants enjoy an average income that leaves their former east bloc allies far behind.

Yet foreign banks have been surprisingly slow to move into the northernmost and wealthiest of the former Yugoslav republics, mercifully spared the fighting that ravaged Slovenia's neighbours to the south.
"To do business here and be profitable is not very easy," said Peter Setzer, chief executive of Ljudska banka, a subsidiary of Austria's Volksbank.
Labyrinthine bureaucracy and strict central bank controls have created an unforgiving business environment for the 30 banks that operate in Slovenia.
A widespread mistrust of foreign ownership makes the task of setting up a successful banking operation even more daunting for outsiders.
So far only four foreign banks have opened their doors in Ljubljana. That compares with about 10 in the Czech Republic and seven in Slovakia.
"The Bank of Slovenia is too protective," said Janusek Sefman, deputy general manager of Banka Societe Generale Ljubljana. "But the legal framework is the minimum condition. We also need good will."

Slovenian ambitions to join the European Union will eventually force the government and central bank to open up the domestic market, analysts say. Until then foreigners will have to live with strict controls.

Slovenia's hawkish central bank currently prohibits foreign financial institutions from opening branch offices. Instead it insists that outsiders put up 680 million tolars ($5 million) to establish a subsidiary then pay an additional 4.08 billion tolars for a full operating licence.

Even then the battle is not over. Banks still have to chart a course through treacherous regulatory waters. Tight controls on foreign currency movements, for example, are designed to maintain the stability of the domestic currency, the tolar.

"There have to be regulations, the Slovenian tolar is only five years old. But this creates problems for us because it makes it more difficult to use foreign exchange savings for credits," said Natasa Pukl at Bank Austria in Ljubljana.
The state-run Slovenian payment agency, which oversees domestic transactions, adds to the banks' headaches by creating additional paperwork.
"It is a mess. All of the banks have to run very costly operations and it is impossible to apply existing (west European) software," said an analyst, who declined to be named.
Austrian banks started what promised to be a goldrush into Slovenia in the early 1990s, eager to expand outside an overcrowded and increasingly unprofitable domestic market.

Bank Austria, the nation's biggest bank, was the first to return to the former Habsburg territory in 1990, rebuilding its operations from scratch. Its predecessor Laenderbank had 13 branches in the Balkans prior to World War One.
Bank Austria's main competitor Creditanstalt-Bankverein followed in 1992, taking a majority stake in Nova banka. Volksbank entered the market one year later when it took over Stajerska banka.
The only non-Austrian, Societe Generale, began offering commercial banking services in 1994.
So far the newcomers have made only limited inroads despite enjoying a certain cache with a public mistrustful of Slovenian banks after two domestic currency crises this century.
Bank Austria has the biggest market share in balance sheet terms, with around two percent. Creditanstalt has nearer one percent.

But all the newcomers say they are committed to Slovenia for the long haul. "We are playing on a long-term basis," said Societe Generale's Sefman. "It is our estimation that Slovenia is small but it has a future."
